title: Agency and contract law
summary: Who a producer represents, the three kinds of authority, what makes a contract valid, and the doctrines courts use to read a policy.
objectives: Tell express, implied and apparent authority apart
Name the elements of a legal contract, with Michigan's rules
Recognize adhesion, aleatory, conditional, unilateral and personal contracts
Separate representation, warranty, concealment, fraud, waiver and estoppel

scenes.title: The Millers sign up: agency and contract law
scenes.subtitle: Who your agent really works for, what makes a contract, and the legal words hiding in every policy

beats.text: Sam and Jen Miller just bought a house in Grand Rapids. Now they're at Dana's desk.
beats.say: Sam and Jen Miller just bought a house in Grand Rapids. Now they're at Dana's desk.

beats.text: Great. Where do I sign?
beats.say: Great. Where do I sign?

draw.text: It depends on which company I place you with.
Appointed by the insurer, selling for it
If placed with a company that never appointed her
For each policy: one side, never both

beats.text: Wait. Dana, whose side are you on: ours, or the insurance company's?
beats.say: Wait. Dana, whose side are you on: ours, or the insurance company's?

beats.text: Fair question. It depends on which company I place you with.
beats.say: Fair question. It depends on which company I place you with.

beats.text: The Millers' insurer appointed Dana, and she sells, solicits and negotiates as its representative. In Michigan, that makes her an agent of the insurer.
beats.say: The Millers' insurer appointed Dana, and she sells, solicits and negotiates as its representative. In Michigan, that makes her an agent of the insurer.

beats.text: If she placed their policy with a company that never appointed her, Michigan would call her an agent of the insured, representing the Millers. For each policy, she's on one side, never both.
beats.say: If she placed their policy with a company that never appointed her, Michigan would call her an agent of the insured, representing the Millers. For each policy, she's on one side, never both.

draw.text: Not Dana's money: she holds it for others

beats.say: Sam hands Dana his first premium. It isn't her money: she holds it for others. Where does it go?

options.label: In her own account, with her money
options.fail: In Michigan, premiums go in a separate account, apart from the agent's own money.

beats.text: Sam's premium lands next to Dana's vacation fund. In Michigan, premiums belong in a separate account.
beats.say: Sam's premium lands next to Dana's vacation fund. In Michigan, premiums belong in a separate account.

beats.text: Now his premium is commingled with her own money.
beats.say: Now his premium is commingled with her own money.

options.label: Treat it as hers until the policy comes
options.fail: In Michigan, an agent is a fiduciary for all money received as agent, and premiums go in a separate account.

beats.text: Dana spends it on pizza at Tony's. No: it's fiduciary money, not hers to spend.
beats.say: Dana spends it on pizza at Tony's. No: it's fiduciary money, not hers to spend.

options.label: In a separate premium account
options.win: In Michigan, an agent is a fiduciary for all money received as agent. Premiums go in a separate account, apart from her own money.

beats.text: Into the premium account it goes. Not my vacation fund!
beats.say: Into the premium account it goes. Not my vacation fund!

beats.text: That's the fiduciary rule.
beats.say: That's the fiduciary rule.

reveal.text: A fiduciary holds money for others. In Michigan, premiums are fiduciary money, segregated from the agent's own funds.
reveal.say: A fiduciary holds money for others. In Michigan, premiums are fiduciary money, segregated from the agent's own funds.

scenes.title: What is Dana allowed to do?
scenes.src: MCL 500.1201(h); IRMI glossary: express, implied authority; apparent agency; Cornell LII Wex; cp-cp_personal-02

draw.text: In Michigan, a license alone gives no authority to act for an insurer
Spelled out, in writing or out loud
Not spelled out: needed for the job, or allowed without objection
What a customer reasonably assumes from the insurer's conduct

beats.text: First, her license. In Michigan, a license alone gives no authority to act for any insurer. That comes from the insurer, in three kinds.
beats.say: First, her license. In Michigan, a license alone gives no authority to act for any insurer. That comes from the insurer, in three kinds.

beats.text: Express is Explained, Implied is Inferred, Apparent is how it Appears.
beats.say: Express is Explained, Implied is Inferred, Apparent is how it Appears.

beats.text: Express authority is spelled out by the insurer, in writing or out loud, like Dana's agency contract.
beats.say: Express authority is spelled out by the insurer, in writing or out loud, like Dana's agency contract.

beats.text: Implied authority isn't spelled out, but it's reasonably necessary for the job, or allowed without objection. Her contract covers auto sales but never mentions ID cards. Handing Rosa hers is implied.
beats.say: Implied authority isn't spelled out, but it's reasonably necessary for the job, or allowed without objection. Her contract covers auto sales but never mentions ID cards. Handing Rosa hers is implied.

beats.text: Watch out: implied is actual authority. Apparent authority is only what a customer reasonably believes from the insurer's conduct. Here's a story.
beats.say: Watch out: implied is actual authority. Apparent authority is only what a customer reasonably believes from the insurer's conduct. Here's a story.

scenes.title: The agent who kept the binders
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: apparent agency; express authority; question core-012
scenes.plain: The power a reasonable person would assume an agent has, based on the insurer's own conduct.
scenes.example: An insurer ends an agent's binding authority but leaves him its sign and blank binders. Tony, reasonably believing the agent can still bind, buys a binder.
scenes.exam: Not express: it was withdrawn. The insurer may be estopped from denying it.

beats.text: In Detroit, an insurer ends an agent's power to issue binders, temporary evidence of coverage. But it leaves its sign on his door, and blank binders.
beats.say: In Detroit, an insurer ends an agent's power to issue binders, temporary evidence of coverage. But it leaves its sign on his door, and blank binders.

beats.text: Tony reasonably believes the agent can still bind, and buys one. That's apparent authority: the power a reasonable person would assume an agent has, based on the insurer's own conduct.
beats.say: Tony reasonably believes the agent can still bind, and buys one. That's apparent authority: the power a reasonable person would assume an agent has, based on the insurer's own conduct.

beats.text: Express? No, it was taken back. But because of its own conduct, the insurer may be estopped, legally blocked, from denying it.
beats.say: Express? No, it was taken back. But because of its own conduct, the insurer may be estopped, legally blocked, from denying it.

scenes.title: Express, implied or apparent?
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: express, implied authority; apparent agency; Cornell LII Wex; NARA glossary; question core-gen-17

cards.text: Dana's agency contract says she may bind homeowners coverage up to $500,000.
cards.why: The power is spelled out in the agency contract: express.

cards.text: The insurer's vice president phones Dana and clearly tells her she may also bind boat policies.
cards.why: Express authority can be given out loud as well as in writing.

cards.text: Dana's contract lets her collect premiums but says nothing about receipts. She hands Sam one.
cards.why: Not spelled out, but reasonably necessary to complete the collection she was allowed to make: implied.

cards.text: Rosa buys a binder from an agent, not knowing his contract ended. The insurer left him its signs and forms.
cards.why: No real authority was left, but the customer reasonably believed it from the insurer's conduct: apparent.

cards.text: For years Dana has issued certificates of insurance without written permission. The insurer never objected.
cards.why: When the insurer doesn't object, the authority is treated as part of the contract: implied.

beats.text: Your turn. Express, implied or apparent? Swipe through five cases.
beats.say: Your turn. Express, implied or apparent? Swipe through five cases.

reveal.text: The tell: granted in words is express. Needed for the job, or allowed without objection, is implied. Only believed from the insurer's conduct is apparent.
reveal.say: The tell: granted in words is express. Needed for the job, or allowed without objection, is implied. Only believed from the insurer's conduct is apparent.

scenes.title: How the Millers' contract is born
scenes.src: Gorham v Peerless (1962); AFT Michigan (2015); MCL 722.52(1); Maids Int'l v Saunders (1997); ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Agreement

draw.text: Banned by statute: void or unenforceable

beats.text: Our Agent Collects Cash Legally: Offer, Acceptance, Consideration, Competent parties, Legal purpose.
beats.say: Our Agent Collects Cash Legally: Offer, Acceptance, Consideration, Competent parties, Legal purpose.

beats.text: Sam fills out the application. In Michigan, that's only an offer, and the insurer's silence generally isn't acceptance.
beats.say: Sam fills out the application. In Michigan, that's only an offer, and the insurer's silence generally isn't acceptance.

beats.text: The insurer accepts by issuing the policy or a binder.
beats.say: The insurer accepts by issuing the policy or a binder.

beats.text: Consideration is what each side gives: the Millers, premium plus compliance with the policy's rules; the insurer, its promise to pay. Don't flip them.
beats.say: Consideration is what each side gives: the Millers, premium plus compliance with the policy's rules; the insurer, its promise to pay. Don't flip them.

beats.text: Competent parties need legal age, in Michigan 18, and mental capacity. And the purpose must be legal: insuring a shipment of illegal drugs is unenforceable. A contract banned by statute is void or unenforceable.
beats.say: Competent parties need legal age, in Michigan eighteen, and mental capacity. And the purpose must be legal: insuring a shipment of illegal drugs is unenforceable. A contract banned by statute is void or unenforceable.

scenes.title: Every policy is served in A CUP, A
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: adhesion, aleatory, unilateral contract; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. C; Secs. I and II Cond. E

spots.label: Adhesion
spots.text: The insurer drafts the policy. The Millers take it or leave it, without bargaining over the wording. So courts read ambiguous wording against the insurer.

spots.label: Conditional
spots.text: The insurer's duty to pay depends on the Millers meeting the policy conditions, like their duties after a loss.

spots.label: Unilateral
spots.text: Only the insurer makes legally enforceable promises. The Millers just meet conditions, like paying the premium and reporting losses.

spots.label: Personal
spots.text: The policy insures the Millers, not the house. If they sell, the policy can't be assigned to the buyer without the insurer's written consent.

spots.label: Aleatory
spots.text: An unequal exchange that depends on chance. One month of premium might buy a huge claim, or years of premium might buy nothing.

beats.text: Every policy is served in A CUP, A: Adhesion, Conditional, Unilateral, Personal, Aleatory.
beats.say: Every policy is served in A CUP, A: Adhesion, Conditional, Unilateral, Personal, Aleatory.

beats.text: Tap the five glowing spots.
beats.say: Tap the five glowing spots.

reveal.text: Watch the two A's: adhesion is about who wrote it; aleatory is the unequal exchange that rides on chance.
reveal.say: Watch the two A's: adhesion is about who wrote it; aleatory is the unequal exchange that rides on chance.

scenes.q: The Millers ask Dana to change a word in their policy. She says the insurer wrote it, so they take it or leave it. This shows the policy is:
scenes.why: Adhesion: the insurer drafts it, and the insured takes it or leaves it without bargaining over the wording. Aleatory is the unequal, chance-driven exchange.

beats.text: The Millers ask to change a word in their policy. Dana says the insurer wrote it: take it or leave it. Which trait?
beats.say: The Millers ask to change a word in their policy. Dana says the insurer wrote it: take it or leave it. Which trait?

reveal.text: Adhesion: the insurer wrote it, and the Millers take it or leave it.
reveal.say: Adhesion: the insurer wrote it, and the Millers take it or leave it.

scenes.title: How a court reads the policy
scenes.src: IRMI glossary; Wilkie v Auto-Owners Ins Co, 469 Mich 41 (2003); NARA glossary: indemnity; questions core-020, core-gen-27

draw.text: Read against the insurer, who wrote it
Some courts: yes. Michigan declined it
Two policies still pay no more than $50,000
Both sides presumed to disclose all pertinent facts

beats.text: If a word in a policy could mean two things, that's an ambiguity. Courts read it against the insurer, which wrote it.
beats.say: If a word in a policy could mean two things, that's an ambiguity. Courts read it against the insurer, which wrote it.

beats.text: Some courts give the coverage an insured would reasonably expect: the reasonable expectations doctrine. Michigan declined to adopt it, but on the exam, that's still its name.
beats.say: Some courts give the coverage an insured would reasonably expect: the reasonable expectations doctrine. Michigan declined to adopt it, but on the exam, that's still its name.

beats.text: Indemnity puts you back where you were before the loss, without profit. Two policies on a loss of $50,000 still pay no more than $50,000.
beats.say: Indemnity puts you back where you were before the loss, without profit. Two policies on a loss of fifty thousand dollars still pay no more than fifty thousand dollars.

beats.text: And insurance runs on utmost good faith: both sides are presumed to disclose all pertinent facts.
beats.say: And insurance runs on utmost good faith: both sides are presumed to disclose all pertinent facts.

scenes.src: IRMI glossary: representation, warranty, concealment, fraud; MCL 500.2218(1), (2); NARA glossary: fraud

draw.text: To the best of my knowledge...

beats.text: Four voices fill out an application.
beats.say: Four voices fill out an application.

beats.text: To the best of my knowledge.

beats.say: A warranty, guaranteed true. It voids the policy if it's untrue.

beats.text: You didn't ask.
beats.say: You didn't ask.

beats.say: Concealment: willfully holding back pertinent facts the insurer didn't ask about.

beats.say: Gotcha!

scenes.title: Sam's basement question
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: concealment, misrepresentation, uberrimae fidei; MCL 500.2218(1), (2); questions core-018, core-gen-30

beats.text: The application never asks about water. But the seller told Sam the basement floods every spring. What does he do?
beats.say: The application never asks about water. But the seller told Sam the basement floods every spring. What does he do?

options.label: Say nothing. They didn't ask!
options.fail: Concealment is willfully holding back pertinent information, even though the insurer didn't ask. It can void the policy.

beats.text: Sam zips his lip. That's concealment, and it can void the policy, even though nobody asked.
beats.say: Sam zips his lip. That's concealment, and it can void the policy, even though nobody asked.

options.label: Write: Bone dry. Never a drop!
options.fail: A false statement to the insurer is a misrepresentation. In Michigan, it can void the policy if material: the insurer would have refused had it known.

beats.text: Sam writes bone dry, knowing it floods. That's an intentional misrepresentation. In Michigan, a material one can void the policy. Splash.
beats.say: Sam writes bone dry, knowing it floods. That's an intentional misrepresentation. In Michigan, a material one can void the policy. Splash.

draw.text: Basement: bone dry. Never a drop! Sam
Can void the policy, if material

options.label: Tell Dana about the flooding
options.win: Utmost good faith: both sides are presumed to disclose all pertinent facts, even ones the form doesn't ask about.

beats.text: Heads up, Dana: the basement floods every spring.
beats.say: Heads up, Dana: the basement floods every spring.

beats.text: Honest and complete. That's utmost good faith.
beats.say: Honest and complete. That's utmost good faith.

reveal.text: The rule: disclose pertinent facts, even unasked, and never write what you know is false.
reveal.say: The rule: disclose pertinent facts, even unasked, and never write what you know is false.

scenes.title: Sam pays late, again
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: estoppel; waiver; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Secs. I and II Cond. B; question core-019
scenes.plain: You can't go back on your own conduct when someone reasonably relied on it.
scenes.example: For years the insurer took Sam's late premiums. Then it tries to cancel him for paying late. It may be estopped.
scenes.exam: Watch out: waiver is chosen, a known right given up on purpose. Estoppel is imposed because someone relied. 2011 HO form: waivers in writing.

draw.text: Waiver: in writing, by the insurer

beats.text: Three years later, Sam often pays late, and the insurer keeps taking his premiums.
beats.say: Three years later, Sam often pays late, and the insurer keeps taking his premiums.

beats.text: They always took my late payments. I figured late was fine.
beats.say: They always took my late payments. I figured late was fine.

beats.text: Then it tries to cancel him for paying late. Estoppel: you can't go back on conduct someone reasonably relied on.
beats.say: Then it tries to cancel him for paying late. Estoppel: you can't go back on conduct someone reasonably relied on.

beats.text: Sam relied on it, so the insurer may be estopped from canceling for late payment. The law says stop.
beats.say: Sam relied on it, so the insurer may be estopped from canceling for late payment. The law says stop.

beats.text: Its cousin, waiver, is a choice: you wave goodbye to a known right on purpose. Watch out: waiver is chosen; estoppel is imposed because someone relied. The 2011 homeowners form requires waivers in writing by the insurer.
beats.say: Its cousin, waiver, is a choice: you wave goodbye to a known right on purpose. Watch out: waiver is chosen; estoppel is imposed because someone relied. The twenty eleven homeowners form requires waivers in writing by the insurer.

beats.text: Remember: in Michigan, a producer not appointed by the insurer writing the policy is an agent of the insured. Express is explained, implied is inferred, apparent is how it appears. Contracts need offer, acceptance, consideration, competent parties and legal purpose.
